beats.narration: Begin by framing Introduction to Raster Graphics Pipeline as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. The OpenGL graphics pipeline processes vertices through programmable shader stages. Consider this worked case: A triangle mesh is passed to vertex shaders that compute position and normal attributes for each vertex. On screen, display a flowchart showing vertex input -> vertex shader -> primitive assembly -> clipping -> rasterization -> fragment shader -> framebuffer. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.
beats.title: Introduction to Raster Graphics Pipeline
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a flowchart showing vertex input -> vertex shader -> primitive assembly -> clipping -> rasterization -> fragment shader -> framebuffer.

beats.narration: Now define Primitive Assembly and Clipping precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Primitive assembly groups vertices into points, lines, or triangles. Consider this worked case: A polygon with one vertex outside the camera frustum is clipped to intersect the view volume boundaries. On screen, show a 3-D polygon being clipped by a view frustum, highlighting the clipped-out segment and the resulting clipped primitive. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Primitive Assembly and Clipping
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a 3-D polygon being clipped by a view frustum, highlighting the clipped-out segment and the resulting clipped primitive.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Rasterization and Interpolation operates in a concrete sequence. Interpolation produces per-fragment values from vertex outputs. Consider this worked case: A triangle is rasterized into a set of pixels, with color and normal values interpolated across each pixel based on barycentric coordinates. On screen, illustrate a triangle being rasterized into a grid of pixels, with color gradients showing interpolated vertex attributes. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Rasterization and Interpolation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a triangle being rasterized into a grid of pixels, with color gradients showing interpolated vertex attributes.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Fragment Processing and Depth Testing and make the decision criteria explicit. Depth testing resolves visibility according to stored depth values. Consider this worked case: A backface-occluded triangle is discarded because its depth value is greater than the stored depth buffer value at that pixel. On screen, show a depth buffer comparison where a closer triangle overwrites a farther triangle's pixel values. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Fragment Processing and Depth Testing
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a depth buffer comparison where a closer triangle overwrites a farther triangle's pixel values.

beats.narration: Apply Blending and Coordinate Spaces to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Coordinate spaces, sampling, and numerical precision must remain explicit. Consider this worked case: A semi-transparent overlay is blended with the underlying scene using alpha blending to produce a final pixel color. On screen, demonstrate alpha blending by showing a transparent shape merging with a solid background, highlighting the alpha channel calculation. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Blending and Coordinate Spaces
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Demonstrate alpha blending by showing a transparent shape merging with a solid background, highlighting the alpha channel calculation.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Geometric Modeling and Transformations, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Computer graphics uses geometric models to represent objects and scenes. Consider this worked case: A 3-D model is translated, rotated, and scaled using transformation matrices to position it in the scene. On screen, show a 3-D object being transformed through space, with axes and matrix values displayed alongside the transformed geometry. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost. Name each dependency explicitly, and keep labels and representations consistent throughout the analysis.
beats.title: Geometric Modeling and Transformations
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a 3-D object being transformed through space, with axes and matrix values displayed alongside the transformed geometry.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Viewing and Projection with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Viewing maps a scene through a camera model to an image. Consider this worked case: A perspective projection matrix converts 3-D world coordinates into 2-D screen coordinates, simulating camera depth. On screen, illustrate a camera model projecting 3-D scene geometry onto a 2-D image plane, showing the projection matrix in action. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.
beats.title: Viewing and Projection
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Illustrate a camera model projecting 3-D scene geometry onto a 2-D image plane, showing the projection matrix in action.

beats.narration: Use Shading and Texture Mapping to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Texture mapping associates image data with geometric surfaces. Consider this worked case: A diffuse shading model computes surface brightness based on light direction and surface normal, while a texture map applies a 2-D image to a 3-D surface. On screen, show a 3-D surface with diffuse shading and a texture overlay, highlighting the light direction and normal vector calculations. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Shading and Texture Mapping
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a 3-D surface with diffuse shading and a texture overlay, highlighting the light direction and normal vector calculations.

beats.narration: Connect Hardware Shaders and Rasterization Focus to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. The course will focus on rasterization techniques and emphasize the hardware rasterization pipeline including the use of hardware shaders. Consider this worked case: A fragment shader computes lighting and color values for each pixel in parallel on the GPU, accelerating rasterization. On screen, display a GPU architecture diagram highlighting shader cores processing fragment data during the rasterization stage. Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.
beats.title: Hardware Shaders and Rasterization Focus
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a GPU architecture diagram highlighting shader cores processing fragment data during the rasterization stage.

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Visual correctness follows from explicit conventions, assumptions, sampling decisions, and measurable error. Consider this worked case: A renderer checks anti-aliasing, depth precision, and sampling rates to ensure measurable error remains within acceptable bounds. On screen, show a checklist graphic with items like 'Verify depth buffer precision', 'Check sampling rates', 'Validate coordinate transformations', and 'Measure visual error'. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.
beats.title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a checklist graphic with items like 'Verify depth buffer precision', 'Check sampling rates', 'Validate coordinate transformations', and 'Measure visual error'.

sources.author: Rochester Institute of Technology
sources.excerpt: Foundations of Computer Graphics is a study of the hardware and software principles of interactive raster graphics. Topics include an introduction to the basic concepts, 2-D and 3-D modeling and transformations, viewing transformations, projections, rendering techniques, graphical software packages and graphics systems. The course will focus on rasterization techniques and emphasize the hardware rasterization pipeline including the use of hardware shaders. Students will use a standard computer graphics API to reinforce concepts and study fundamental computer graphics algorithms. Programming projects and a survey of the current graphics literature will be required. Note: students who complete CSCI-510 may not take CSCI-610 for credit. sources.author: Khronos Group
sources.excerpt: The OpenGL graphics pipeline processes vertices through programmable shader stages. Primitive assembly groups vertices into points, lines, or triangles. Clipping removes portions outside the view volume. Rasterization converts primitives into fragment candidates. Interpolation produces per-fragment values from vertex outputs. Fragment processing computes values for framebuffer operations. Depth testing resolves visibility according to stored depth values. Blending combines a fragment result with an existing framebuffer value. Coordinate spaces, sampling, and numerical precision must remain explicit.
sources.title: OpenGL Specification and Reference

sources.author: MIT OpenCourseWare
sources.excerpt: Computer graphics uses geometric models to represent objects and scenes. Transformations position and orient geometry within coordinate systems. Viewing maps a scene through a camera model to an image. Rasterization samples projected primitives on a discrete pixel grid. Shading models how light, material, and geometry determine appearance. Texture mapping associates image data with geometric surfaces. Curves and surfaces provide compact smooth shape representations. Animation changes scene state over time. Ray tracing follows visibility and light paths through a scene. Visual correctness follows from explicit conventions, assumptions, sampling decisions, and measurable error.
